newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ SPORT-CRICKET- Watch out for Mullally, Lloyd warns.
newsitem.headline: NZ SPORT-CRICKET- Watch out for Mullally, Lloyd warns.

text.p: AUCKLAND, Jan 22 - England cricket coach David Lloyd believes left-arm swing bowler Alan Mullally will play a crucial role at some point in their three-test series against New Zealand, NZPA reported on Wednesday.

With all the attention focused on whether new-ball king Dominic Cork wins his race against time to be fit for Friday's first test at Eden Park, Lloyd yesterday gave a vote of confidence to the tall Mullally's talents.
He has played the last eight tests since making his debut against India last year and has taken 25 wickets. Now Lloyd wants him to step up a gear against New Zealand.
"I've a hunch Mullally will bowl somebody (team) out," he said.
"He's strong and he's using the new ball to good effect. He's got the challenge to turn dependability and stock bowling into match-winning performances."
Mullally warmed up for the first test with four for 52 in Northern Districts' second innings on Monday and, irrespective of Cork's injury worries, he seems sure to make the side for Eden Park.
The 27-year-old Mullally has trod an interesting path to the England team.
Born in Southend, Essex, his parents emigrated to Perth when he was a child and he played junior grade cricket there.
When he was 18, Mullally was called into the Western Australia side for his debut -- in the 1987-88 Sheffield Shield final victory over Queensland.
He played 15 first-class matches for the state, taking 37 wickets at an unflattering 42.05.

But he always intended making his mark in England, and after a brief flirtation with Hampshire, joined Leicestershire, for whom he took 70 wickets in last year's county championship at an impressive 25.34.
With his height, Mullally can get bounce from any pitch and displayed sharp in-swing against Northern Districts.
He has his goals in sight in New Zealand, and for the remainder of his test career.
"I want to achieve a minimum four or five wickets per test, then you're up with the best of them," he told NZPA.
Mullally made it clear the England team in New Zealand was a refreshed invigorated group of players compared with the unhappy discontented squad in Zimbabwe a month ago.
Mullally described his Christmas Day as consisting of a ham and cheese toasted sandwich, phone calls with his parents and girlfriend and watching CNN on television.
"The boys couldn't wait to get away from Zimbabwe," he said.
"Don't get me wrong, it wasn't a bad place, but the pitches were low and slow and negative and produced negative sort of cricket.
"These pitches in New Zealand bring the bowlers into the game a lot more and make for better cricket."
Mullally is sure England will be a far more combative competitive unit in New Zealand.
Two convincing wins over a Selection 11 and Northern Districts gave their tour of New Zealand a strong start and Mullally believes England can go on from there in the test series.
"The boys are now playing as they should be playing," he said.
"We are a lot better side than people keep saying. If we're not playing well people have the right to criticise.
"Now we are playing much better, hopefully we'll win in New Zealand and that'll put us in good stead for the Ashes series this year."
